_comment: Tunable reference data for victim_profile.py — the VICTIM-SIDE analysis used when an operator serves their content from hostnames they do not own (hijacked subdomains, compromised CMS, dangling records). The question this layer answers is NOT 'who is the operator' but 'what capability did the operator need to obtain these hostnames'. The victim set is evidence: if the victims share a control panel, the operator has an exploit; if they share a provider, that provider is breached; if they share NOTHING technical, the operator is working from stolen or purchased credentials. GENERIC public knowledge only — panel/CMS/provider constants, thresholds. NEVER case data (contributor RULE 1). Edit freely; it is a STARTER set, not exhaustive.

panel_dns_signatures._comment: Hosting control panels auto-create predictable subdomains in a customer's zone when the zone is provisioned. Their PRESENCE on a victim apex identifies the panel PASSIVELY, from DNS alone, with no probing of the victim (who is not our target and should not be scanned). Match is on the leftmost label of a subdomain of the victim apex. A victim whose panel cannot be identified is 'unknown', never 'none' — absence of the label is weak evidence.

panel_host_signatures._comment: Reverse-DNS / default-vhost hostname suffixes that identify the panel on the SERVER side (i.e. on the attacker's box, or on a shared host). Substring match against a PTR record or a default certificate CN. Useful for confirming the panel the operator themselves runs, which is a separate question from the panel each victim runs.

managed_dns_operators._comment: DNS operators large enough that two victims sharing one is NOT a link. Matched against the nameserver suffix of the victim apex. A victim set concentrated on one of THESE still tells you little; a victim set concentrated on a small regional host is far more meaningful. Keep in sync conceptually with tools/kb noise_filters managed_dns_suffixes — this list serves a different question (concentration weighting, not edge suppression), so it is deliberately separate.

hypotheses._comment: The access-vector hypotheses this layer discriminates between, in the order they are tested. Each names the victim-set SHAPE that supports it and the shape that refutes it, so an analyst can audit the call. 'concentration' is the largest share of victims sitting on one value of that dimension (0.0-1.0). These are DECISION AIDS with explicit thresholds, not verdicts — the tool reports the shape and the supported hypothesis; the analyst writes the judgment.

provider_breach._comment: One hosting/DNS provider is itself compromised, or an insider is adding records. Supported when nearly all victims are customers of ONE provider that is NOT a hyperscale managed DNS operator. Refuted the moment a victim at an unrelated provider appears — which is why widening the victim sweep is the single highest-value move in this analysis.

panel_exploit._comment: A vulnerability (or default/weak credential) in one control-panel product. Supported when one panel dominates the victim set ACROSS SEVERAL DIFFERENT PROVIDERS — provider diversity is what separates this from provider_breach. Chase the panel's version banner next; a version-locked victim set is close to proof. BASE-RATE WARNING: cPanel is the default panel on the large majority of the world's shared hosting, so a cPanel-dominated victim set is close to what you would get by drawing shared-hosting domains at random. Treat a cPanel concentration as SUPPORTED ONLY IF you can also show a version or a specific vulnerable component in common; without that it is a base-rate artifact, not a finding. A concentration on a MINORITY panel (Plesk, DirectAdmin, CyberPanel, ISPConfig) is far more informative than the same number on cPanel.

cms_exploit._comment: A CMS or plugin vulnerability giving file/DNS write access. Supported when one CMS dominates across several providers. Weaker than it looks: a WordPress-dominated victim set may only reflect WordPress's ~40% share of the web, so compare the observed share against the sector's base rate before asserting.

reseller_or_agency._comment: One web agency, reseller or IT contractor holds delegated access to all the victims and has been compromised. Supported when victims share a small non-managed DNS operator or a common technical contact while differing in registrar, country and panel. Often the explanation when victims are all in one country and one business sector.

credential_supply._comment: The operator holds STOLEN or PURCHASED panel/DNS credentials for many unrelated victims — infostealer log corpora and initial-access-broker listings are the usual supply. This is the DEFAULT conclusion when every other hypothesis fails, and it is a positive finding, not a shrug: dispersion ACROSS providers, countries, panels and sectors is exactly the signature of a credential list, because a list has no technical common factor. Corroborate with onset clustering — a tight compromise window suggests one bulk dump was worked through; a spread suggests ongoing access or a drip-fed broker relationship.

thresholds._comment: Global tuning for the profiler. 'min_victims_for_any_call' guards against reading a pattern into two or three victims — with a tiny victim set every dimension looks concentrated by chance, and the honest output is 'insufficient victims'. 'onset_tight_days' is the window within which several victim compromises count as one campaign push (evidence of a bulk credential dump being worked through) rather than opportunistic drip.

victim_sectors._comment: Coarse business-sector keywords matched against the victim apex label and page title, used only to test whether the victim set is sector-concentrated (which would point at a shared agency, a sector-specific CMS, or a targeted list) rather than sector-random (which points at an indiscriminate credential dump). Deliberately crude — this is a concentration test, not a business classifier.
